source.name: C++ for DV Interviews (NVIDIA RDSS Prep)

questions.title: Find the maximum and second maximum (distinct) of an array in one pass
questions.prompt:
Given `vector<int> a`, return the largest value and the second-largest **distinct** value in a single pass.

- Input `[3, 7, 7, 5, 9, 1]` -> output `(9, 7)`
- Input `[4, 4]` -> output `(4, none)` (no second distinct value)
- Input `[]` -> `(none, none)`

Then port it to SystemVerilog.
questions.answer: One pass, two variables: if `x > first` shift first into second; else if `x < first && x > second` update second. O(n) / O(1). Follow-up: duplicates of the max (skip `x == first`), what if second doesn't exist (flag or `std::optional`).

questions.title: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place and return the new length
questions.prompt:
Given a **sorted** `vector<int>& a`, remove duplicates in place so the first `k` elements are the unique values in order, and return `k`. O(1) extra space.

- `[1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]` -> `k = 4`, `a` starts with `[1, 2, 3, 4]`
- `[]` -> `0`; `[5]` -> `1`
questions.answer: Read and write pointers: `k = 1`; for each `i`, if `a[i] != a[i-1]` then `a[k++] = a[i]`. O(n) / O(1). Follow-up: allow each value twice; unsorted input -> `unordered_set`.

questions.title: Find the element that appears exactly once
questions.prompt:
1. Given `vector<int> a`, return the **first** element (in input order) that appears exactly once, or -1 if none. Example: `[5, 3, 5, 9, 3, 7]` -> `9`.
2. Special case: every element appears exactly twice except one. Solve it in O(1) extra space. Example: `[4, 1, 2, 1, 2]` -> `4`.
questions.answer: General: `unordered_map` count, then a second pass in input order: O(n) / O(n). If all others appear exactly twice: XOR everything (`x ^ x = 0`, `x ^ 0 = x`), O(1) space. Follow-up: two unique elements (split by a set bit of the XOR).

questions.title: Build a frequency table of every element, then return the top-k most frequent
questions.prompt:
Given `vector<int> a`:
1. return the count of every distinct value;
2. return the `k` most frequent values with their counts, most frequent first.

Example: `a = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]`, `k = 2` -> `[(1, 3), (2, 2)]`.
questions.answer: `unordered_map<int,int>` with `m[x]++` (operator[] default-constructs 0): O(n) / O(k distinct). Top-k: copy to a vector and `partial_sort` by count, O(n + d log k). Trap: `m[k]` inserts missing keys; use `find`/`count` for lookups.

questions.title: Reverse a string in place (std::string and C char*)
questions.prompt:
1. Reverse a `std::string` in place. `"hello"` -> `"olleh"`.
2. Same for a NUL-terminated C string `char* s` (no library calls).
questions.answer: Two pointers from both ends, `swap(s[i++], s[j--])` while `i < j`: O(n) / O(1). C version: walk to the `'\0'`, then swap. Cast `size()-1` to int so an empty string doesn't underflow.

questions.title: Check whether two strings are anagrams
questions.prompt:
Given two lowercase strings `a` and `b`, return true if `b` is a rearrangement of `a`.

- `"listen"`, `"silent"` -> true
- `"rat"`, `"car"` -> false
questions.answer: `int cnt[26]`: increment for `a`, decrement for `b`, fail as soon as a count goes negative; length check first. O(n) / O(1). Follow-ups: Unicode (hash map or sort), group anagrams (sorted string as key).

questions.title: Count UVM_INFO / UVM_WARNING / UVM_ERROR / UVM_FATAL messages in a simulation log
questions.prompt:
Read a simulation log file line by line and count each UVM severity. Do **not** count the end-of-test report summary lines (`UVM_ERROR :    1`).

Input:
```text
UVM_INFO tb.sv(42) @ 100: uvm_test_top [TEST] test started
UVM_ERROR sb.sv(88) @ 520: uvm_test_top.env.sb [SB] addr mismatch
UVM_WARNING mon.sv(10) @ 900: ... timeout approaching
--- UVM Report Summary ---
UVM_INFO :    1
UVM_ERROR :    1
```
Output: `UVM_INFO=1 UVM_WARNING=1 UVM_ERROR=1`.
questions.answer: `ifstream` + `getline` (streams, O(1) memory per line); split the first two tokens with `istringstream`; count when the first token is a severity and the second is not `":"`. Faster variant: `line.compare(0, 9, "UVM_ERROR") == 0`. Follow-ups: 20 GB log (stream, avoid regex, early exit), top-5 messages, first error timestamp.

questions.title: Extract and insert a bit field with uint32_t masks
questions.prompt:
Write
- `get_field(x, hi, lo)`: return bits `[hi:lo]` of a 32-bit value;
- `set_field(x, hi, lo, v)`: return `x` with bits `[hi:lo]` replaced by `v`.

Examples: bits `[5:3]` of `0b11010110` -> `2`; `set_field(0xABCD1234, 15, 8, 0x5A)` -> `0xABCD5A34`.
questions.answer: Shift then mask: `(x >> lo) & ((1u << (hi-lo+1)) - 1)`. Insert: `(x & ~(m << lo)) | ((v & m) << lo)`. Use unsigned fixed-width types and `1u`; a 32-bit-wide field needs a guard (`1u << 32` is UB). SV: `x[hi:lo]`.

questions.title: Model a bounded FIFO as a C++ class (deque-based and ring buffer)
questions.prompt:
Implement a FIFO with a fixed depth: `push`, `pop`, `full`, `empty`.
1. using `std::deque` (template on the element type);
2. as a circular buffer with read/write pointers, like RTL.

Example (depth 2): push 10, push 20, push 30 (rejected: full), pop -> 10, push 30, pop -> 20, pop -> 30.
questions.answer: `deque`: `push_back` / `front` + `pop_front`, full when `size() == depth`; throw or return false on overflow/underflow. Ring buffer: `buf[depth]`, `rd`, `wr`, `count`, indices wrap with `% depth`; `count` plays the role of the extra pointer bit RTL uses to tell full from empty. O(1) per op.

questions.title: Group AXI channel events by transaction ID and find incomplete transactions
questions.prompt:
Given a list of `(id, channel)` events in arrival order, group the channels per ID and report IDs whose write never completed (no `B` response).

Input: `{(1,"AW"), (2,"AW"), (1,"W"), (3,"AW"), (2,"W"), (1,"B")}`
Output: `1: AW W B`, `2: AW W`, `3: AW`; incomplete = `{2, 3}`.
questions.answer: `map<int, vector<string>> by_id; by_id[tid].push_back(ch);` (ordered map for sorted printing): O(n log n) / O(n). Incomplete = IDs whose vector has no `"B"`. Follow-up: out-of-order checks (per-ID queues, see scoreboard).

questions.title: Set, clear, toggle and test bit n; isolate/clear the lowest set bit; check power of two
questions.prompt: For a `uint32_t x`, write one-line expressions to set, clear, toggle and test bit `n`, isolate the lowest set bit, clear the lowest set bit, and check whether `x` is a power of two. Show them on `x = 0x68`.
questions.answer: Set `x |= 1u << n`; clear `x &= ~(1u << n)`; toggle `x ^= 1u << n`; test `(x >> n) & 1u`; lowest set bit `x & (~x + 1)`; clear lowest `x & (x - 1)`; power of two `x && !(x & (x - 1))`. SV: `x[n]`, `$onehot(x)`.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** every single-bit operation is a mask `1u << n` combined with OR (set), AND-NOT (clear), XOR (toggle) or shift-AND (test). The two "lowest set bit" tricks come from how `x - 1` flips the trailing zeros and the lowest 1.

| Task | C++ | SystemVerilog |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Set bit n | `x \|= (1u << n)` | `x[n] = 1'b1` |
| Clear bit n | `x &= ~(1u << n)` | `x[n] = 1'b0` |
| Toggle bit n | `x ^= (1u << n)` | `x[n] = ~x[n]` |
| Test bit n | `(x >> n) & 1u` | `x[n]` |
| Lowest set bit | `x & (~x + 1)` | `x & -x` |
| Clear lowest set bit | `x & (x - 1)` | `x & (x - 1)` |
| Power of two | `x && !(x & (x - 1))` | `$onehot(x)` |

Worked example, `x = 0x68 = 0110 1000`:

| expression | binary | hex |
| --- | --- | --- |
| x | 0110 1000 | 0x68 |
| x - 1 | 0110 0111 | 0x67 |
| x & (x - 1) | 0110 0000 | 0x60 (lowest 1 cleared) |
| ~x + 1 (= -x) | 1001 1000 | 0x98 (low byte) |
| x & -x | 0000 1000 | 0x08 (lowest 1 isolated) |
| power of two? | x & (x-1) != 0 | no |
| x \| (1u << 0) | 0110 1001 | 0x69 |
| x ^ (1u << 5) | 0100 1000 | 0x48 |

### Code
```cpp
#include <cstdint>

inline uint32_t set_bit(uint32_t x, unsigned n)    { return x |  (1u << n); }
inline uint32_t clear_bit(uint32_t x, unsigned n)  { return x & ~(1u << n); }
inline uint32_t toggle_bit(uint32_t x, unsigned n) { return x ^  (1u << n); }
inline bool     test_bit(uint32_t x, unsigned n)   { return (x >> n) & 1u; }
inline uint32_t lowest_set(uint32_t x)             { return x & (~x + 1u); }
inline uint32_t clear_lowest(uint32_t x)           { return x & (x - 1u); }
inline bool     is_pow2(uint32_t x)                { return x && !(x & (x - 1u)); }
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `1 << 31` with a signed `1` is UB: use `1u`. Shifting by >= 32 is UB too.
- `is_pow2(0)` must be false: that is what the `x &&` guards.
- In SV `$onehot(0)` is false and `$onehot0(0)` is true.

### Follow-ups
- **Hamming distance (LeetCode 461)?** `popcount(a ^ b)`.
- **Counting bits for 0..n (LeetCode 338)?** `bits[i] = bits[i & (i - 1)] + 1`.

questions.title: Count the set bits of a 32-bit value (popcount)
questions.prompt: Return the number of 1 bits in a `uint32_t`. Example: `0xB4` (`1011 0100`) -> `4`. Give the Brian Kernighan loop and mention the built-ins.
questions.answer: Kernighan: `while (x) { x &= x - 1; n++; }` loops once per set bit. Built-ins: `__builtin_popcount(x)`, C++20 `std::popcount`. SV: `$countones(x)`.

questions.title: Compute the parity of a 32-bit value (loop and O(log n) fold)
questions.prompt: Return true if a `uint32_t` has an **even** number of 1 bits. Write a simple loop and an O(log n) XOR-fold version. Example: `0xB4` has four 1s -> even parity -> true.
questions.answer: Loop XOR of every bit, or fold: `x ^= x>>16; x ^= x>>8; x ^= x>>4; x ^= x>>2; x ^= x>>1; return !(x & 1);`. Built-in `__builtin_parity`. SV: `^x` (odd), `~^x` (even).

questions.title: Reverse the bits of an 8-bit value
questions.prompt: Write `uint8_t reverse8(uint8_t x)` that mirrors the bit order. Example: `0b1101_0010` (`0xD2`) -> `0b0100_1011` (`0x4B`).
questions.answer: Loop 8 times: `r = (r << 1) | (x & 1u); x >>= 1;`. SV: streaming operator `{<<{x}}`. Follow-up: 32-bit swap-halves trick (LeetCode 190).

questions.title: Convert binary to Gray code and back
questions.prompt: Write `bin2gray(b)` and `gray2bin(g)` for `uint32_t`. Example: `5 (101)` -> Gray `7 (111)`; Gray `7` -> `5`. Explain why async FIFO pointers use Gray code.
questions.answer: `gray = b ^ (b >> 1)`. Back: `for (; g; g >>= 1) b ^= g;` (each binary bit is the XOR of all Gray bits above and including it). One bit changes per increment, so a synchronizer never samples a torn multi-bit value.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Gray code changes **exactly one bit** between consecutive values. Encoding is one XOR with the shifted value; decoding XORs together all higher Gray bits (a prefix XOR from the MSB down).

| n | binary | Gray | bits changed from n-1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 000 | 000 | |
| 1 | 001 | 001 | 1 |
| 2 | 010 | 011 | 1 |
| 3 | 011 | 010 | 1 |
| 4 | 100 | 110 | 1 |
| 5 | 101 | 111 | 1 |
| 6 | 110 | 101 | 1 |
| 7 | 111 | 100 | 1 |
| 0 (wrap) | 000 | 000 | 1 |

Decode trace `gray2bin(7)`: b = 0 ^ 111 = 111, then ^ 011 = 100, then ^ 001 = **101 = 5**.

### Code
```cpp
#include <cstdint>

uint32_t bin2gray(uint32_t b) { return b ^ (b >> 1); }

uint32_t gray2bin(uint32_t g) {
    uint32_t b = 0;
    for (; g; g >>= 1) b ^= g;       // b = g ^ g>>1 ^ g>>2 ^ ...
    return b;
}
```

### SV port
```systemverilog
function automatic logic [3:0] bin2gray(logic [3:0] b);
  return b ^ (b >> 1);
endfunction

function automatic logic [3:0] gray2bin(logic [3:0] g);
  for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) gray2bin[i] = ^(g >> i);   // XOR of bits i and above
endfunction
```

### Explanation
- **Why Gray in async FIFOs:** the pointer crosses clock domains through a 2-flop synchronizer. If only one bit changes, a metastable sample resolves to either the old or the new pointer, both valid. A binary 3 -> 4 (`011 -> 100`) changes 3 bits and could be sampled as any of 8 values.
- Gray is only one-bit-per-step for power-of-two ranges (the wrap 7 -> 0 is also one bit).

### Follow-ups
- **Assertion?** `$countones(gray ^ $past(gray)) <= 1` on the source clock.
- **Generate the n-bit Gray sequence (LeetCode 89)?** `for i in 0..2^n-1: i ^ (i >> 1)`.

questions.title: Check the machine's endianness and byte-swap a 32-bit value
questions.prompt:
1. Write `is_little_endian()` without library calls.
2. Write `bswap32(x)`: `0x11223344` -> `0x44332211`.
3. Explain why register models use masks rather than bit-field structs.
questions.answer: `uint32_t v = 1; return *reinterpret_cast<uint8_t*>(&v) == 1;` (low byte at the lowest address = little endian). Byte swap with shifts and masks or `__builtin_bswap32`. Bit-field order and padding are compiler-dependent, masks are portable.

questions.title: Parse a key=value line into a map
questions.prompt: Parse a line like `TEST=axi_write STATUS=FAIL ERROR=timeout` into `{TEST: axi_write, STATUS: FAIL, ERROR: timeout}`. Tokens without `=` are skipped.
questions.answer: `istringstream` splits on whitespace; for each token `find('=')`, skip if `npos`, else `out[item.substr(0, eq)] = item.substr(eq + 1)`. Know `string::npos`, `substr(pos, len)`.

questions.title: Extract time, tag and message from every UVM_ERROR line with std::regex
questions.prompt:
From a log, collect every `UVM_ERROR` as `{time, tag, message}`.

Input line: `UVM_ERROR sb.sv(88) @ 520: uvm_test_top.env.sb [SB] addr mismatch`
Output: `{520, "SB", "addr mismatch"}`.
Follow-up: print the 5 most common error messages.
questions.answer: `static const regex re(R"(^UVM_ERROR \S+\(\d+\) @ (\d+): \S+ \[(\w+)\] (.*))");` built once outside the loop; `regex_search(line, m, re)` then `stol(m[1]), m[2], m[3]`. `regex_search` matches anywhere, `regex_match` the whole string. Raw strings avoid double escaping. Top-5: count in a map, copy to a vector, `partial_sort`.

questions.title: Summarize a regression: PASS/FAIL per test log in a directory, then write a CSV
questions.prompt: A directory contains one `.log` per test. A test FAILS if its log has any `UVM_ERROR` or `UVM_FATAL` message (not counting the report summary). Print a table sorted by test name and write `report.csv` with columns `test,status`.
questions.answer: C++17 `std::filesystem::directory_iterator`, filter `.log`, reuse `count_severity`, `bad = c["UVM_ERROR"] + c["UVM_FATAL"]`, store in `std::map` (sorted by name). Write with `ofstream` (closes itself, RAII).

questions.title: Check balanced brackets with a stack
questions.prompt:
Given a string containing `()[]{}` (and other characters), return true if every bracket is closed by the matching type in the right order.

- `"{[()]}"` -> true
- `"([)]"` -> false
- `"(("` -> false
questions.answer: Push openers; on a closer, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener, then pop. At the end the stack must be empty. O(n) / O(n).

questions.title: Reverse a singly linked list in place
questions.prompt: Given `struct Node { int val; Node* next; };` and the head of `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> null`, reverse the list in place and return the new head (`3 -> 2 -> 1 -> null`).
questions.answer: Three pointers: `prev = nullptr`; while `head`: save `nxt = head->next`, point `head->next = prev`, advance `prev = head`, `head = nxt`. Return `prev`. O(n) / O(1).

questions.title: Write an out-of-order scoreboard: in order within an ID, any order across IDs
questions.prompt:
Implement a scoreboard class with:
- `write_expected(id, data)` from the reference model,
- `write_actual(id, data)` from the monitor,
- `check_empty()` at end of test.

Responses with the same ID must arrive in order; different IDs may interleave (AXI rule). Report unexpected IDs, data mismatches and missing responses.
questions.answer: `unordered_map<int, deque<uint32_t>> exp_`: push expected per ID, on actual `find(id)`; error if missing or empty, else compare with `front()` and `pop_front()`. `check_empty()` reports IDs with leftover entries (dropped responses). SV: `bit [31:0] exp_q[int][$]`.

questions.title: Pointer vs reference in C++?
questions.answer: A pointer can be null and reseated; a reference must bind once and can't be null.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** a **pointer** is an object holding an address: it can be null, reassigned, and needs explicit dereferencing. A **reference** is an alias: it must be initialized, can never be null (in valid code), and can't be reseated.

| | Pointer `T*` | Reference `T&` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can be null | yes | no |
| Must be initialized | no | yes |
| Can be reseated | yes (`p = &b`) | no (`r = b` assigns to the referent) |
| Syntax | `*p`, `p->x` | `r`, `r.x` |
| Arithmetic | yes (`p + 1`) | no |
| Typical use | optional/ownership, arrays, C APIs | function parameters (`const T&`), operator overloads |

```cpp
int a = 1, b = 2;
int* p = &a;   p = &b;   *p = 5;     // p now points to b; b == 5
int& r = a;    r = b;                // assigns b's value (5) to a; r still aliases a
void scale(vector<int>& v);          // modify the caller's vector, no copy
void print(const vector<int>& v);    // read-only, no copy
```

### Follow-ups
- **SV equivalent?** SV class handles behave like pointers without arithmetic (can be `null`, reassigned); `ref` arguments in SV tasks/functions behave like C++ references.
- **Dangling reference?** Returning a reference to a local variable: UB once the function returns.

questions.title: struct vs class in C++?
questions.answer: Only the default access differs: `struct` members (and base classes) are public by default, `class` members are private.

questions.title: Pass by value vs pass by const reference in C++?
questions.answer: By value copies the object; `const&` avoids the copy and forbids changes.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** pass by **value** copies the argument (the callee gets its own object); pass by **`const&`** passes an alias without copying and the compiler forbids modification. For large objects (`vector`, `string`, `map`) use `const&` unless you modify or need a copy.

| Signature | Copies? | Callee can modify caller's object? | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `f(vector<int> v)` | yes, O(n) | no (modifies its copy) | needs its own copy / will move from it |
| `f(const vector<int>& v)` | no | no | read-only large inputs |
| `f(vector<int>& v)` | no | yes | in-place algorithms (remove_dups) |
| `f(int x)` | yes (cheap) | no | small scalars |

```cpp
int sum(const vector<int>& a) {          // no copy of a million ints
    int s = 0;
    for (int x : a) s += x;
    return s;
}
void sink(string s) { store_ = std::move(s); }   // by value + move is idiomatic for sinks
```

### Follow-ups
- **Interviewers notice** `f(vector<int> a)` for read-only inputs: say "const ref to avoid the copy".
- **SV?** Arguments are copied by default (`input`); `ref` passes by reference; `const ref` gives read-only by reference. Class handles are copied, but the object isn't.

questions.title: What is a virtual function in C++?
questions.answer: Call resolved at runtime through the vtable; enables polymorphism (same as SV `virtual`).

questions.title: Function overloading vs overriding?
questions.answer: Overload = same name, different parameters, resolved at compile time. Override = a derived class replaces a virtual function, resolved at runtime.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **overloading** is several functions with the same name but different parameter lists in the same scope, picked at **compile time**. **Overriding** is a derived class redefining a base-class **virtual** function with the same signature, picked at **runtime**.

| | Overloading | Overriding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | same scope | base and derived classes |
| Signature | must differ in parameters | must match (covariant return allowed) |
| Needs `virtual` | no | yes (in the base) |
| Resolved | compile time | runtime (vtable) |
| Example | `print(int)`, `print(string)` | `Txn::print()` vs `AxiTxn::print()` |

```cpp
void log(int x);                    // overloads
void log(const string& s);

struct Base    { virtual void run() const; };
struct Derived : Base { void run() const override; };   // override

// Pitfall: name hiding. Derived::log(double) hides all Base::log overloads
// unless you add: using Base::log;
```

### Follow-ups
- **SV?** SV has **no** function overloading; it has overriding of `virtual` methods (and parameterized classes for type genericity).

questions.title: What is a pure virtual function / abstract class?
questions.answer: `virtual void f() = 0;` makes the class non-instantiable; derived classes must implement it (SV: `pure virtual` in a `virtual class`).

questions.title: Why does a polymorphic base class need a virtual destructor?
questions.answer: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer otherwise skips the derived destructor (UB, leaks).

questions.title: Shallow vs deep copy in C++ (and the rule of three)?
questions.answer: The default copy copies pointers, so two objects share one buffer (double delete). Write a copy constructor/assignment (rule of three) or use `vector` / smart pointers. UVM link: handle assignment vs `copy()`/`clone()`.

questions.title: Stack vs heap memory in C++?
questions.answer: Locals live on the stack and die at scope exit; `new` allocates on the heap and needs `delete` (prefer RAII / smart pointers).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **stack** storage is automatic: allocated on function entry, freed at scope exit, very fast, limited size. **Heap** storage is dynamic: allocated with `new`/`malloc`, lives until explicitly freed, any size, slower.

| | Stack | Heap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Allocation | automatic (locals) | `new` / `make_unique` / `malloc` |
| Lifetime | until scope exit | until `delete` / owner destroyed |
| Speed | pointer bump | allocator call |
| Size | small (often 8 MB per thread) | large |
| Bugs | returning address of a local, stack overflow | leaks, double free, use-after-free |

```cpp
void f() {
    int x = 5;                          // stack
    int big[10'000'000];                // likely stack overflow
    int* p = new int[1000];             // heap, must delete[]
    auto v = std::vector<int>(1000);    // object on stack, elements on heap, freed automatically
    delete[] p;
}
int* bad() { int y = 1; return &y; }    // dangling: y died with the frame
```

### Follow-ups
- **RAII?** Tie heap lifetime to a stack object (`vector`, `unique_ptr`, `ifstream`) so cleanup happens at scope exit, even on exceptions.
- **SV?** Class objects come from `new()` and are garbage collected; automatic variables in automatic tasks/functions behave like stack locals.

questions.title: unique_ptr vs shared_ptr?
questions.answer: `unique_ptr`: single owner, freed at scope exit, move-only. `shared_ptr`: reference-counted shared ownership, freed when the last owner goes away.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** both free memory automatically. `unique_ptr` expresses **sole ownership** (move-only, zero overhead); `shared_ptr` expresses **shared ownership** with an atomic reference count; the object dies when the count reaches 0.

| | `unique_ptr<T>` | `shared_ptr<T>` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owners | exactly one | many |
| Copy | no (move only) | yes, increments count |
| Overhead | none vs raw pointer | control block + atomic refcount |
| Create | `make_unique<T>(...)` | `make_shared<T>(...)` |
| Pitfall | | reference cycles leak: break with `weak_ptr` |

```cpp
auto u = std::make_unique<AxiTxn>();
// auto u2 = u;               // error: not copyable
auto u2 = std::move(u);       // ownership transferred, u is null

auto s1 = std::make_shared<AxiTxn>();
auto s2 = s1;                 // use_count() == 2
s1.reset();                   // still alive via s2
```

### Follow-ups
- **Default choice?** `unique_ptr`; switch to `shared_ptr` only when ownership is genuinely shared.
- **SV analog?** Every class handle is like a garbage-collected shared reference.

questions.title: What does static mean in C++ (in a function and in a class)?
questions.answer: In a function: the local keeps its value between calls (initialized once). In a class: one copy shared by all objects. At file scope: internal linkage.

questions.title: What does volatile mean in C/C++, and when do you use it?
questions.answer: Every access really reads/writes memory (no caching in registers or elimination); used for memory-mapped hardware registers. It is not a synchronization primitive for threads.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `volatile` tells the compiler the value can change (or the access has side effects) outside the program's view, so **every read and write must be performed** exactly as written: no caching in registers, no removing "redundant" accesses.

```cpp
// Memory-mapped register access
volatile uint32_t* const CTRL   = reinterpret_cast<volatile uint32_t*>(0x40000000);
volatile uint32_t* const STATUS = reinterpret_cast<volatile uint32_t*>(0x40000004);

*CTRL |= 1u << 0;                    // set enable bit (read-modify-write)
while ((*STATUS & 1u) == 0) { }      // poll: without volatile this may become an infinite loop
```

| Without `volatile` the compiler may | Effect on hardware |
| --- | --- |
| hoist the STATUS read out of the loop | poll never sees the change |
| merge two writes to a FIFO data register | one write lost |
| delete a read whose result is unused | read-to-clear side effect lost |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `volatile` is **not** atomic and gives no memory ordering between threads: use `std::atomic` for that.
- Read-modify-write on a register with write-1-to-clear bits can clear other bits accidentally.

### Follow-ups
- **DV link:** this is exactly what firmware running on a CPU model does in SoC-level tests; the register sequence in C mirrors the UVM CTRL-write / STATUS-poll sequence.

questions.title: What is sizeof a struct, and why is it often bigger than the sum of its members?
questions.answer: Includes padding for alignment, so `struct {char c; int i;}` is usually 8, not 5. Order members largest first to reduce padding.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** each member must sit at an address that is a multiple of its **alignment**, and the struct size is rounded up to a multiple of its largest member's alignment. The compiler inserts **padding** to satisfy both.

`struct A { char c; int i; };` on a typical 64-bit ABI:

| offset | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| content | c | pad | pad | pad | i | i | i | i |

`sizeof(A) == 8`, not 5.

```cpp
struct A { char c; int i; };              // 8
struct B { char a; int i; char b; };      // 12: 1 + 3 pad + 4 + 1 + 3 tail pad
struct C { int i; char a; char b; };      // 8: reorder largest first
struct __attribute__((packed)) P { char c; int i; };   // 5, but unaligned access

static_assert(sizeof(A) == 8);            // typical, not guaranteed by the standard
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Padding is ABI-specific: don't `memcpy` a struct onto a wire format or a register map; serialize field by field.
- Packed structs can cause slow or faulting unaligned accesses on some CPUs.

### Follow-ups
- **SV contrast:** a `packed struct` in SV has no padding at all: it is exactly the sum of its bit widths, laid out MSB first.

questions.title: Why does for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) never terminate?
questions.answer: `size_t` is unsigned, so `i >= 0` is always true and `i--` from 0 wraps to a huge value (and `n - 1` with n == 0 is already huge).

questions.title: Signed vs unsigned integer overflow in C++?
questions.answer: Signed overflow is undefined behavior for `int`; unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** unsigned arithmetic is defined to **wrap modulo 2^N**. Signed overflow is **undefined behavior**: the compiler may assume it never happens and optimize accordingly, so "it wraps on my machine" is not a guarantee.

| expression | type | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UINT32_MAX + 1u` | `uint32_t` | 0 (defined wrap) |
| `0u - 1u` | `unsigned` | `UINT_MAX` |
| `INT_MAX + 1` | `int` | **UB** |
| `(int8_t)200` | conversion | implementation-defined before C++20, -56 since C++20 |
| `1 << 31` | `int` | UB before C++20 |

```cpp
int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;            // can overflow for large indices: UB
int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;       // safe

// Compiler exploits UB: this loop may be compiled as infinite
for (int i = 1; i > 0; i *= 2) { }

uint32_t a = 0xFFFFFFFFu, b = a + 1u;   // b == 0, well defined
```

### Follow-ups
- **Detect it?** `-fsanitize=undefined` (UBSan) or `__builtin_add_overflow`.
- **SV contrast:** SV integer arithmetic is fully defined: results are truncated to the target width (two's complement wrap), signed or not; the classic SV trap is instead *width* (8-bit x 8-bit in an 8-bit context).

questions.title: i++ vs ++i: is there a difference?
questions.answer: Same effect for `int` (the compiler optimizes both); `++i` avoids creating a temporary copy for iterators and class types, so prefer it in loops.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** both increment. `i++` (post-increment) returns the **old** value, so for class types (iterators) it must make a **copy**; `++i` (pre-increment) returns the incremented object itself. For plain `int` in a loop the generated code is identical.

| | `++i` | `i++` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Value of the expression | new value | old value |
| Class types | returns `*this` | copies, increments, returns the copy |
| In `for (...; ...; X)` with `int` | same code | same code |
| Preferred for iterators | yes | no |

```cpp
int i = 5;
int a = ++i;    // i = 6, a = 6
int b = i++;    // i = 7, b = 6

// Typical implementation for an iterator type
It& operator++()    { advance(); return *this; }          // pre
It  operator++(int) { It tmp = *this; advance(); return tmp; }   // post: extra copy

for (auto it = m.begin(); it != m.end(); ++it) { }        // idiomatic
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `a[i] = i++;` and `i = i++ + 1;` were UB before C++17 (unsequenced); avoid modifying a variable twice in one expression.

### Follow-ups
- **SV?** `i++` and `++i` exist in SV too (blocking semantics); avoid them on variables shared between processes in RTL.
